newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Russia, Brazil in focus.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Russia, Brazil in focus.

text.p: Investors must decide this week whether to reduce exposure to emerging markets amid growing concern that a strong January performance could be reversed, analysts said.
They said some markets had registered daunting gains so far this year, and a raft of U.S. figures could spark a correction, especially in Europe.

"There are six or seven bits of data next week. If they come in on the high side it could be the catalyst for the start of a sell-off," said Nigel Rendell, HSBC James Capel emerging market strategist.
Among U.S. figures due for release are the Purchasing Managers Survey on Monday, leading indicators on Tuesday, and unemployment and payrolls on Friday.

RUSSIA faces another week of watching President Boris Yeltsin to determine his state of health. On Sunday he met French President Jacques Chirac in Yeltsin's first direct encounter with a Western leader since his release from hospital.
Chirac said he was impressed with the speed of Yeltsin's recovery.
Russian equities have had a strong run so far in 1997, rising some 40 percent in dollar terms, and Rendell said investors could cash in on those gains if further uncertainty arose.

Investors will also be watching events in the Balkans after more than 10 weeks of demonstrations in SERBIA turned violent at the weekend, when autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic sent in riot police to break up protests.

Marchers have been calling for the reinstatement of opposition victories in local elections last November. Analysts see little prospect of progress on restructuring its outstanding debt in the near term.
In TURKEY, analysts expect another volatile week but say the short-term trend is positive.

They say a consolidation is inevitable following gains of over 60 percent in dollar terms in the IFC emerging market index so far this year, but upward momentum appears likely to leave stocks higher on a net basis at least this week.
HUNGARY is likely to be dominated by company results, all of which must be reported by February 15.
"Most of the companies are not expected to produce particularly spectacular results...They will be closely watched and there could be some profit-taking," an analyst said.
POLAND's market outlook has dimmed amid concern about monetary tightening, analysts said, with a strong GDP figure last week reigniting fears that the economy is growing too fast.
"On Poland, we are a bit more cautious after the rise in the reserve requirement," said Rendell. The National Bank of Poland last week announced an increase in mandatory reserves for banks.
BULGARIA, following losses in the Brady bond market last week amid concern about a possible default on debt servicing, faces continued volatility amid political uncertainty.
There are signs that the ruling Socialists would concede to demands for early elections in the face of major public unrest.

An analyst said early elections could see the reformist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) gain a sweeping mandate to implement reform, with the International Monetary Fund coming up with the funds to put a currency board in place.
In Latin America, ARGENTINA could dominate after the success of its peso-denominated Eurobond issue.
"It is seen as international recognition of the convertibility plan," said Laurie Meister-Melka, Latam director at Robert Flemings.
She said Argentina and MEXICO were the two markets most likely to be affected by U.S. data in the week, but most markets should take their lead from domestic events.
In BRAZIL, political factors should dominate as President Fernando Henrique Cardoso continues his push to become Brazil's first re-elected leader.

An amendment to the constitution to allow him to seek re-election was passed by Brazil's lower house of Congress on Tuesday. The amendment needs a second vote by the lower house before proceeding to the Senate. The second lower-house vote is due around the middle of the month.
Andrew Shores, strategy head at Brazilian investment bank Garantia, said the vote opened the way for the government to proceed with long-awaited structural reform.
The International Finance Corporation's composite index of emerging market equities, denominated in dollars IFC/IPRD, was up 0.3 percent week-on-week at 315.42 at the start of play on Monday.
Latin America fell 0.8 percent over the week to 586.80, Asia was flat at 261.18, and Europe, Middle East and Africa as a region was down 0.1 percent at 149.87.
